A_target.statement:
Let $M = \struct {E, \II}$ be a [[Definition:Matroid|matroid]] and $w: E \to \R$ a weighting.
Then the [[Definition:Greedy Algorithm|greedy algorithm]] computes an [[Definition:Independent Set (Matroid)|independent set]] of maximum weight.

B_source.statement:
Let $V$ be a [[Definition:Vector Space|vector space]].
If $I, J \subseteq V$ are [[Definition:Linearly Independent Set|linearly independent]] with $\card I < \card J$, then there exists $x \in J \setminus I$ such that $I \cup \set x$ is linearly independent.

substitutions.linear independence of vectors: membership in an abstract family of independent sets
substitutions.the exchange property for vector spaces: the exchange axiom taken as a defining condition
substitutions.the rank of a set of vectors: the rank function of the matroid

derived.all maximal independent subsets having e: all bases of the matroid have the same cardinality
derived.the greedy construction of a basis: optimality of greedy for any weight function

object_map.reformulation: Take the exchange property as the definition of independence rather than deriving it from vectors.

validity_conditions: Linear independence satisfies the axioms, so vector matroids are instances and the abstraction is faithful.
The exchange axiom is what forces all maximal independent sets to have the same size, which is what makes greedy well behaved.
The abstraction is strictly wider: graphic and transversal matroids are not all representable over every field, and some matroids are representable over no field at all.
proof_plan: Take the exchange property of [[Definition:Linearly Independent Set|linear independence]] as an axiom.
Define a [[Definition:Matroid|matroid]] by a family $\II$ of independent sets with $\O \in \II$, closed under subsets, and satisfying the [[Definition:Matroid Augmentation Axiom|exchange axiom]].

If $B_1, B_2$ are maximal independent with $\card {B_1} < \card {B_2}$, exchange gives $x \in B_2$ with $B_1 \cup \set x \in \II$, contradicting maximality.
Hence all maximal independent sets have equal size.

Let the greedy algorithm pick $g_1, g_2, \ldots$ in decreasing weight, adding each element that keeps the set independent.
If some basis $B$ had greater weight, let $k$ be the first index with $\map w {b_k} > \map w {g_k}$.
Exchange between $\set {g_1, \ldots, g_{k - 1} }$ and $\set {b_1, \ldots, b_k}$ gives an element the greedy algorithm would have chosen, a contradiction.
{{qed}}
